claims.claim: Sort every cell in your body by size, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120 (Hatton et al., PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, 2023), full text read at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10523466/ and https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML
claims.note: Abstract: 'a surprising inverse relation between cell size and count ... such that all cells within a given logarithmic size class contribute an equal fraction to the body's total cellular biomass'; Results: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class (Fig. 4A)'; Conclusion: 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class'. 'Roughly' matches the paper; outside the fat/muscle gap 'all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude' while size spans seven. Holds for male, female and child ('broadly similar'), so 'your body' is fair. Edge: the binning leaves out platelets and haploid sperm (below red blood cells), so 'every cell' is slightly broad, but those few grams do not change the claim.

claims.claim: Hook as seen by a viewer who swipes away at second two: if you group your body's cells by size, each size group holds roughly the same total weight.
claims.where: spoken + on-screen: hook card 'ROUGHLY THE SAME' (A4)
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120 (Hatton et al., PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, 2023), full text read at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10523466/ and https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML
claims.note: This is the paper's headline finding (Significance: 'cellular biomass in any given logarithmic cell-size class ... approximately independent of cell size'). The viewer who leaves early does not hear about the dip, but the paper itself states the pattern with 'roughly'/'approximately' and treats the gap as an irregularity within it, so the early impression is not false.

claims.note: Overstates.
